answer_text:
Great question! Switching the US to the metric system would be **extremely difficult** — and it's not just stubbornness holding it back. Here's a comprehensive breakdown:

---

## 🏛️ A Long History of Failed Attempts

The US has caught a lot of grief for never switching to the metric system, but the fact is, it tried several times. U.S. customary units have been defined in terms of metric units since the 19th century, and the US actually has a national policy to adopt the metric system. In 1866, Congress authorized the use of the metric system and the nation officially recognized it, but did not mandate its use. In 1975, the Metric Conversion Act promoted metrication, but it was not mandatory — it left adoption up to individual industries, and without legal compulsion, few sectors saw the benefit of making the switch.

---

## 💰 The Cost Problem

The biggest reasons the US hasn't adopted the metric system are simply time and money. The US retains the imperial system primarily due to the immense economic costs of converting industrial, manufacturing, and transportation infrastructure. Additionally, deep-rooted familiarity, a lack of mandatory federal adoption, and the logistical challenge of replacing billions of dollars' worth of equipment make the transition impractical.

For a sense of scale: We only have to look to Canada to get a sense of what switching would take. Canada went metric back in 1970, and it took about 15 years and more than $1 billion to update everything. The US is vastly larger, so costs would be far higher. Every speed limit sign would have to be changed from miles per hour to kilometers per hour — and so would every sign on every city street, country road, and freeway across the nation.

The costs associated with a full conversion of NASA's measurement systems alone would be $370 million, including all measurement software and tools that would have to be modified in the transition.

---

## 🏭 Industrial & Infrastructure Inertia

When the Industrial Revolution began, expensive manufacturing plants became a main source of American jobs. Because the Imperial System was in place at this time, the machinery used in these factories was developed in Imperial units, all of the workers were trained with Imperial units, and many products were made to feature Imperial units.

Today, with mass production of goods, switching everything over to a new measurement system would be a gigantic undertaking. The US switching to metric this late in the game would be by far the largest, most complex transition of measurement systems in human history.

---

## 🧠 Cultural Resistance

The simple answer for why America hasn't gone full-on metric is that the overwhelming majority of Americans have never wanted to. Whenever the discussion of switching arose in Congress, the passage of a bill favoring the metric system was thwarted by big businesses and American citizens who didn't want to go through the time-consuming and expensive hassle of changing the country's entire infrastructure. Labor unions were among the strongest opponents of 1970s-era metrication, fearing that the switch would make it easier to ship jobs offshore.

---

## ⚠️ Safety Risks During Transition

Switching could also be dangerous. A famous plane mishap happened back in 1983 during Canada's transition to the metric system. In the US, a similar confusion caused a catastrophe: the root cause for the loss of NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter spacecraft was the failure to use metric units in the coding of a ground software file. Over the course of the probe's nine-month journey, this caused it to arrive around 170 kilometers lower than planned — costing NASA $125 million.

---

## ✅ The US Is Already More Metric Than You Think

Despite all this, American manufacturers have put out all-metric cars, and the wine and spirits industry abandoned fifths for 750-milliliter bottles. The metric system is, quietly and behind the scenes, now the standard in most industries, with a few notable exceptions like construction. Many US industries heavily use the metric system, especially those with international ties, including science, medicine, automotive, electronics, and manufacturing. Examples include pharmaceutical dosages in milligrams, automotive parts in millimeters, and consumer products with dual-labeled packaging.

---

## 🔑 Bottom Line

A full, mandatory switch to the metric system in the US would be **enormously difficult** — requiring decades of effort, tens of billions of dollars, retraining of workers, replacement of infrastructure, and overcoming deep cultural resistance. There are obvious benefits, like the simplicity of metric, getting on the same standard as the rest of the world, and reducing conversion errors — but the political will and public appetite for such a massive upheaval has never materialized.
